tagline: Cottonwoods along the St. Joe lead toward a mountain climb
intro: The St. Joe River Scenic Byway follows Forest Highway 50 east from St. Maries, tracing a cottonwood-lined river before climbing to the Montana border. It is a paved, two-lane road with numerous pullouts. Visit Idaho promotes the scenic byway for birdwatching and fishing; bald eagles and osprey use the riverside cottonwoods. Its 2024 guide gives a length of 87.3 miles and a driving time of two hours, 21 minutes.

Water transport helped establish St. Maries: Joseph Fisher selected a mill site near the two rivers, and the sawmill was first built in 1889. Logs floated to mills, while steamboats carried finished products to market. Steamboat passengers nicknamed the slow stretch between St. Joe City and St. Maries the Shadowy St. Joe for the cottonwoods reflected in its water. In the 1930s, the Civilian Conservation Corps built the Gold Creek-Little Joe Road, opening the upper St. Joe area to motor vehicles. The Gold Creek-Little Joe Road climbs to Gold Summit in the Bitterroot Mountains.

From St. Maries, travel upriver past Marble Creek’s logging displays to Avery’s railroad depot. At the junction with Road 218, Forest Highway 50 turns north for the climb to the Idaho-Montana border; Red Ives Ranger Station lies south on Road 218.

moments.title: Marble Creek
moments.text: Marble Creek’s interpretive displays focus on the problem of moving western white pine logs out of the drainage to mills on the St. Joe River. They explain early-1900s logging technology and the people who lived and worked here.

moments.title: Avery
moments.text: At Avery, the Milwaukee Road changed locomotives between electric power and steam or diesel. The town served as a division point on the railroad’s Pacific Extension. During the Great Fire of 1910, the U.S. Army’s 25th Infantry Regiment, known as the Buffalo Soldiers, helped build the backfire that saved Avery. Many people took refuge in newly built railroad tunnels northeast of town. The depot later passed to the town after the railroad’s bankruptcy; it now serves as a community center, museum, post office and library. The wood-frame depot has a passenger waiting area at one end and a freight room at the other, with the agent’s office between them.

moments.title: Red Ives Ranger Station
moments.text: Red Ives Ranger Station takes its name from a red-haired prospector. The Forest Service established the station in 1935, when the Civilian Conservation Corps built the first roads into the area. The station lies ten miles south of the St. Joe River Scenic Byway on Forest Service Road 218.

practical: Avery: The archived Visit Idaho guide says the Avery-to-border section is usually open May through November and becomes a snowmobile route in winter. (checked 2026-10-11)
